segments.name: standby
say: A PC that's switched off is still sipping power.
A coin cell keeps its clock ticking, and the power supply's standby rail keeps part of the chipset awake, with one small chip watching the power button.

segments.name: press
say: Press it, and a single green wire tells the power supply to switch on.

segments.name: power-good
say: The supply ramps its rails, then deliberately waits up to a quarter of a second before promising the power is stable.
It's the longest single wait before the CPU runs anything.

segments.name: csme
say: Inside the chipset, another computer boots first: Intel's security engine, a 32-bit core based on the 486.
Inside the chipset, another computer boots first: Intel's security engine, a thirty-two-bit core based on the four eighty-six.
It loads signed firmware from the same flash chip as the BIOS, sets up the clocks, and only then lets the main processor out of reset.
It loads signed firmware from the same flash chip as the bye-oss, sets up the clocks, and only then lets the main processor out of reset.

segments.name: reset
say: Reset lifts, and every core runs its reset microcode.
One hardware thread is chosen to lead: the bootstrap processor.
The other 31 halt, powered and listening, until software sends them a start-up message.
The other thirty-one halt, powered and listening, until software sends them a start-up message.

segments.name: microcode
say: Before its very first instruction, the processor patches itself.
It finds a table in flash and loads a microcode update into every thread, on every boot, because a hard reset wipes the last one.

segments.name: boot-guard
say: On PCs with Boot Guard, an Intel-signed module runs next, from inside the cache, and checks the firmware before letting it run.
So on those machines, the first x86 code isn't 16-bit at all.
So on those machines, the first x eighty-six code isn't sixteen-bit at all.

Its first instruction sits sixteen bytes below 4 GiB.
Its first instruction sits sixteen bytes below four gigabytes.
There's no RAM yet, and the caches are off. So the fetch leaves the die, crosses to the chipset, and is read out of the flash chip that holds the firmware.

segments.name: far-jump
say: The code wears 1978 clothes, but already reaches for 1985 parts.
The code wears nineteen seventy-eight clothes, but already reaches for nineteen eighty-five parts.
It loads a tiny table of segments, sets one bit in a control register, and makes a far jump.

segments.name: cache-as-ram
say: It's a 386 now, but it still has no RAM to put anything in.
It's a three eighty-six now, but it still has no ram to put anything in.
So the firmware borrows the cache.
It points it at addresses where no memory exists, then switches on No-Eviction Mode, so those lines can never be thrown out.
768 KiB of RAM, made of cache.

segments.name: first-call
say: Now there's a stack, and for the first time since reset, the processor makes a call.
From here on, the firmware is written in C.

segments.name: eye
say: Next it has to teach the DDR5 memory to talk.
Next it has to teach the D D R five memory to talk.
At these speeds a bit lasts under 180 picoseconds, so every byte lane needs its own timing.
At these speeds a bit lasts under a hundred and eighty picoseconds, so every byte lane needs its own timing.
The firmware sweeps timing and voltage, testing at each setting, and parks each lane in the middle of the passing region: the eye.

segments.name: first-boot
say: With about fifty training steps, a first boot with new DDR5 typically sits on a black screen for tens of seconds.
With about fifty training steps, a first boot with new D D R five typically sits on a black screen for tens of seconds.
On a normal boot, the saved results are simply restored.

segments.name: leave-cache
say: Memory works, and everything worth keeping is copied into it.
Then the firmware does something no normal program ever should: it throws away the entire cache, without writing anything back.

segments.name: doorbell
say: Now it wakes the other 31 threads, all at once.
Now it wakes the other thirty-one threads, all at once.
Each starts as an 8086, climbs to 32-bit protected mode in about a dozen instructions, reports in, and parks.
Each starts as an eighty eighty-six, climbs to thirty-two-bit protected mode in about a dozen instructions, reports in, and parks.

segments.name: smm
say: Then, one at a time, each is sent into System Management Mode to move its private save area.
Entering that mode drops a thread back to something like real mode, so every future visit repeats the climb.

segments.name: long-mode
say: On this board, everything so far, even memory training, ran as 32-bit code.

segments.name: wake-again
say: The other threads are woken yet again, and this time climb all the way to 64-bit.
The other threads are woken yet again, and this time climb all the way to sixty-four-bit.
For each of them, that's at least the third climb this boot.

segments.name: dxe
say: DXE is a small operating system in its own right: on this board, 260 drivers, inflated from flash into memory.
Dixie is a small operating system in its own right: on this board, two hundred and sixty drivers, inflated from flash into memory.
And all of it runs on one thread, of one core.

segments.name: pcie
say: Then it walks the PCI Express buses, reading the first four bytes of every possible device.

All ones means nobody's home; anything else is a vendor and device ID.

segments.name: gop
say: Once the firmware has locked itself down, the graphics card's own driver runs, on the CPU, not the GPU.
The boot logo is just pixels written into the card's memory.

segments.name: boot-loader
say: Then it picks something to boot, checks its signature, and runs the boot loader, still leaning on the firmware to read the disk.

segments.name: exit
say: The kernel calls ExitBootServices, and the firmware steps aside.
The kernel calls Exit Boot Services, and the firmware steps aside.
The other 31 threads sit in a tiny halt loop, waiting to be woken again.
The other thirty-one threads sit in a tiny halt loop, waiting to be woken again.
